better anticipation and management of restructuring would help employees and companies to adapt to the transitions imposed by globalisation. management and employee representatives are the main actors who need to agree on company-wide restructuring strategies. such restructuring should, however, be accompanied by policy interventions to avoid social problems and promote new skills and jobs. this can avoid massive redundancies and the decline of entire regions or the complete relocation of industrial sectors. for example, the recent departure of a major company from romania was a hasty one, without a proper analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of this relocation, without taking firm guarantees for the social protection of the employees who were left without jobs. i therefore thank the rapporteur for this complex report, which analyses these situations in depth and seeks general solutions.
i congratulate mr cercas on his report. economic growth is based on creating and maintaining jobs in europe, and these depend on the development of european industry. we call on the commission to re-examine the union's industrial and competitiveness policy, including through the lens of security and accessibility of energy and raw materials supplies. in mr cercas' report, parliament asks the commission to examine whether it is necessary to take measures at european level to supervise the activities of undertakings in order to avoid any kind of abuse involving damage, in particular to workers. i think that in restructuring situations it is important for the company to consult not only the unions in the location where the restructuring is taking place but all the unions in the locations where the company produces on european territory. we ask the commission to present as soon as possible, after consulting the social partners, a proposal for a legal act on the information and consultation of workers.
at european level, the main objective of the information and consultation of workers is to strengthen social dialogue with a view to ensuring a coherent package of social measures in all member states. this will certainly lead to the prevention and management of restructuring processes, especially in this difficult period of economic and social crisis, which is felt in all areas. i consider it important to set a general minimum framework of the necessary requirements relating to the right of workers to be informed and consulted throughout the community and in line with the guidelines of the 2020 strategy on social policies. we know that when a restructuring decision is taken, the process as such does not affect just one company, as companies work more in networks. measures taken at european level to prevent such situations for both workers and employers must therefore be robust and limit the impact of restructuring.
question for the blue card. i would like to ask our esteemed colleague if the youth unemployment rate is the only thing that worries her. i think we should also be concerned about the drop-out rate, because both youth unemployment and the drop-out rate are putting the future of the european union at risk. that is why i believe that a priority for the european union, the commission and the member states should be not only to provide quality education and training to ensure vocational qualifications, but above all to create jobs.
among the european employment problems, high youth unemployment is one of the most pressing, as it has a negative impact on the demographic situation as well as on social systems. the introduction of the youth guarantee at member state level would be a huge step towards reversing these trends, but the measure also raises a number of questions. at present, the form of financing that would allow all member states to introduce the youth guarantee is not in sight, as esf resources are already in place and member states' budgets are concentrated on deficit reduction targets. perhaps even more questionable is the lack of consultation with potential partners - public authorities, industry representatives, educational institutions - which would have to be done by each member state individually, and without which such a programme cannot succeed. the youth guarantee could play an important role in mitigating the impact of the european economic situation on young generations, but its implementation poses serious problems due to the lack of preparation and dedicated funds.

mr president, the debate about the future of europe has now reached a crucial stage. the european institutions, member states and politicians are focusing increasingly on economic, financial and monetary issues, which are no doubt of major importance. nevertheless, together with my fellow citizens from eastern europe, i find myself asking: what will post-crisis europe look like? are macroeconomic indicators more important than fundamental values? is it acceptable to slightly disregard the rule of law if one achieves a balanced budget? we eastern europeans lived through the fall of the iron curtain and rushed immediately towards a european union of values. we were eager to reunite with those not forced by history to experience totalitarianism. we are now worried that post-crisis europe could downgrade the universal values of human dignity, liberty, equality and solidarity. macroeconomic indicators must never be substituted for european values.
on 1 january 2014, all barriers to the free movement of romanian and bulgarian workers will be lifted. 16 member states have already removed barriers to the free movement of romanian and bulgarian workers, recognising that removing barriers protects both native and migrant workers. i condemn in this regard the irresponsible and anti-european statements made by nigel farage regarding the lifting by the united kingdom, as of 1 january 2014, of barriers to the free movement of romanian and bulgarian workers. the member states must not be afraid to ensure that all workers in the union have a free movement area. the free movement of workers is one of the union's fundamental principles and one of the most cherished benefits created by the european union. i call on the irish presidency of the council of the european union to recommend to the member states that barriers to the free movement of romanian and bulgarian workers be removed as soon as possible.
i want to draw attention once again to the serious deterioration of the situation of the roma. this ethnic group continues to be the most hated and excluded minority in europe. recently, a fascist organization in romania offered a cash reward to roma women who agreed to be sterilized so as to stop procreating beings that they believed were not human but rather animals. but worse, this kind of unqualified extremist discourse is slowly making its way into political movements at the forefront of public life. for example, a founding member of the ruling fidesz party in hungary said that roma are all murderers, animals incapable of human communication and incapable of coexistence. all this is happening while, in the brussels offices, strategies are being written for nicely packaged but ineffective rums, while silence is total when the speech 'anti-gypsyism' comes up. i ask the commission to come up with a proposal for a legal instrument that constantly addresses manifestations of anti-gypsyism.
the schengen area is the essence of the european construction, through the free movement of people and, by implication, goods. in june 2011, the european parliament gave the green light to romania and bulgaria to join the schengen area, following field visits and technical assessments. the rapporteur appointed by parliament and the group of experts concluded that romania fulfilled all the schengen criteria, which had been assumed by the treaty of accession as early as 2005. today, a year and a half after that event, romania and bulgaria are not yet full members of the schengen area. the socialist-liberal government in bucharest seems to have put accession to the background, as the only country that objected was the netherlands, which is still led by a coalition of socialists and liberals. i hope that the romanian government will resolve the external credibility problems which are currently preventing bulgaria from joining schengen, as a senior european official recently said.

over the last ten years, the solidarity fund has been one of the union's successful instruments, but it needs to be re-adapted to provide new and rapid solutions to the sometimes very serious problems facing european citizens. i therefore ask the commission to be clearer and more transparent in setting the scope of the solidarity fund and in defining clearly, simply and precisely what constitutes a disaster and the conditions for its eligibility at regional level for access to the fund. there must be no room for interpretation, clarity is a condition for using this fund in a transparent, fair and controllable way. this will eliminate legal uncertainty and speculation about the eligibility criteria, which in some cases have generated negative attitudes among citizens, who believe that their problems are not wanted to be solved by the union.

in writing. − the solidarity fund has proved to be one of the union's most successful and appreciated instruments, being one of the few instruments available to the union to demonstrate its solidarity and closeness to european citizens. the instrument provides support for emergency operations in the event of a disaster, reduces the financial burden on member states in such situations and allows the union as a whole to show solidarity with its citizens facing a difficult situation. it is necessary to improve the effectiveness of the instrument by reducing the time between a disaster and the granting of aid. administrative procedures are slow, complicated and confusing, but this could be avoided by small changes that would not change the fundamental core of the current union regulation. we need to cut red tape to get the fund. the granting of advances would be very useful and appropriate and the merging of procedures and decisions would contribute to significantly accelerating the current procedure. this instrument should remain outside the union budget, as it is not possible to know in advance to what extent it will be used during the year. the instruments that are to provide a response in exceptional and unforeseen crisis situations must remain extra-budgetary instruments.

in writing. − i voted in favour of the report on the implementation and application of the solidarity fund. this instrument aims to provide financial support to member states and regions affected by major natural disasters and is based on the principle of solidarity enshrined in the treaty. the fund was used both to repair housing damaged by the 2009 earthquake in the abruzzo region and to restore infrastructure damaged by the 2005 floods in austria. in this context, the process of reviewing the financial instrument proposed in this report and aiming at broadening its scope and application is welcomed.
in writing. − the european union solidarity fund has proved its worth during its implementation period, being one of the union's most successful and appreciated instruments. however, from my own experience, i regret to tell you that the current time taken to mobilise the fund is unacceptably long and that for this reason many of the results that were intended to be achieved through the use of this fund have been undermined. as i have said in my amendments, i believe that we urgently need to improve the administrative framework and the procedures for mobilising the fund. this, coupled with the merging of grant decisions and implementing agreements at commission and member state level and the introduction of fixed advance payments as soon as the affected state has requested assistance, will lead to improved effectiveness of the funds and will accelerate the process of assisting states affected by a major disaster.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the european union solidarity fund, implementation and enforcement. the european union solidarity fund (eusf) is the eu's main instrument for responding to major natural disasters and showing solidarity with europe's disaster-stricken regions. i support the need to simplify the bureaucratic processes required to mobilise this eu instrument, so as to reduce the time between the time of the disaster and the time when the affected member state or region receives aid. the majority of solidarity fund assistance applications (63%) were submitted under the exceptional category 'regional disaster', and 66% of these were rejected following the commission's assessment. the regulation provides for special attention to be paid to remote and isolated regions and requires that these criteria be examined by the commission 'with the utmost rigour'. given that both the intensity and frequency of natural disasters in europe have continued to increase, i believe that it is necessary to clearly and simply define regional disasters and to clarify their eligibility.
mr president, the european citizens have a fundamental right to good administration that is key to good governance. people are entitled to a swift and efficient reply to their request. this right is founded in article 41 of the charter of fundamental rights. a regulation on a european law of administrative procedure will make clear the principal of good administration that all institutions must respect. transparency, efficiency, cost efficiency and a unitary practice must be the objectives of this regulation. by giving eu institutions clear guidelines for action, we will improve the union’s administrative capacity. this regulation will create a unitary code of conduct across different institutions and make possible external monitoring. citizens must be able to control the work and practices of the european institutions. this would of course increase direct accountability and also the people’s trust.
in writing. − the lack of a coherent set of codified rules of administrative law in the european union does not facilitate citizens' understanding of their rights under union administrative law. i believe that european legislation on administrative procedural law will help the eu administration to use its internal organisational assets to facilitate and promote the highest standards in administration; will enhance the union's legitimacy and public confidence in the union's administration; will promote cooperation and the exchange of good practice between national administrations and the union's administration.
in writing. − the eu's direct administrative system needs common rules on administrative procedures for efficiency, harmony and transparency. the lack of a coherent set of laws makes it difficult for citizens to engage in direct administration. clearer and faster responses to their requests are needed, which would help to increase public confidence in the european administrative apparatus.
in writing. − the citizens of the european union must have full confidence in the european institutions, because we must not forget that their legitimacy depends precisely on the confidence of eu citizens in the community structures. i believe that the drawing up and adoption of a regulation on administrative procedures will increase the sense of security for the citizens of the union on the one hand, and for the union's officials on the other.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the own-initiative report on the recommendations to the commission on european union administrative procedural law. citizens have the right to transparency, prompt resolution and response from the union administration, whether by lodging a formal complaint or exercising their right to petition under the treaty. at the same time, citizens must be given information on the possible actions they can take in their case. unfortunately, a pressing problem for the eu is a lack of trust from citizens, and a european administrative procedural law would enhance the union's legitimacy and citizens' trust in its administration. a european administrative procedural law would assist the union administration in using its internal organisation powers to facilitate and promote the highest standards of administration. i voted in favour of the request to the commission to submit, under article 298 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, a proposal for a regulation on a european administrative procedural law, following the recommendations of the european parliament.
mr president, the european strategy 2020 states that better anticipation and management of restructuring would help employees and companies to adapt to transition. with the financial crisis, the number of cases of restructuring has been increasing in europe and this has created fear among workers that their own companies might be on the verge of restructuring. this whole climate of insecurity sets up a vicious circle with a great impact on our economy. how can we sustain a dynamic economy if its own actors feel insecure? i call on the commission to take measures to convince companies of the need to inform and consult the relevant local public authorities and workers about their restructuring decisions. however, a directive on the issue is not needed. what companies and workers need are guidelines and good practices to deal with such situations. predictability is one of these.
in writing. − one of the most important problems facing european societies at the moment is the size of unemployment in european economies. beyond the monetary aspects, the scale of this phenomenon significantly calls into question the european union's objective of achieving sustainable, smart and inclusive growth. according to the latest european statistics, the unemployment rate is still above 10%, with more than 20 million european citizens looking for a new job. in these circumstances, it is imperative that economic restructuring processes, imposed by the specific dynamics of markets, be accompanied by processes of information and consultation of the relevant social partners. restructuring processes must take place within a framework that takes into account the social responsibility and implicit effects, for example, in view of increasing the employment opportunities for redundant employees.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because we are in a difficult economic context, where the restructuring of companies implies extremely high costs for employees but also for the local or regional economy. in the current conditions created by the global economic crisis, restructuring of companies unfortunately leads to large-scale layoffs. that is why i believe we need to create a culture in which the management of corporate reorganisation and restructuring is done in a socially responsible way. for this reason, i strongly support the application of concrete rules in this area, both at european and national level. one of the most serious consequences of business restructuring is that young people are among the categories of workers most frequently targeted by redundancies. and this trend is unacceptable, given the extremely high rate of youth unemployment in the eu. it is necessary that all restructuring operations be preceded by adequate information and preparation of all interested parties.
in writing. − i appreciate that there will eventually be a european strategy for managing restructuring processes in a socially responsible way. experience has shown that well-managed restructuring can improve the future of industries, workers, regions and cities affected by technological change, economic crisis or globalisation. the key factors are anticipating change and providing a leadership role in social dialogue. the european commission must present a legislative proposal to minimise social costs, paying particular attention to the most affected sectors and regions. restructuring can be done in a much smarter and longer-term way. as a european issue, we need european legislation to ensure that restructuring is anticipated and managed in a fair and balanced way when it occurs. the commission should present a legal act on anticipation of restructuring, ensuring that minimum requirements exist at eu level when the absence of collective agreements is found during restructuring. the legal act must ensure that all stakeholders are involved in the long-term planning of enterprises, including the social partners as well as local and regional authorities. training must be provided for all workers to anticipate future skills and ensure the competitiveness of the european workforce.
in writing. − the financial and economic crisis has led to a deepening of the social crisis, by increasing the number and impact of restructuring. in this context, i support the report with its recommendations to the commission on informing and consulting workers in order to avoid slipping into a deep recession caused by a dramatically high unemployment rate. the social dialogue needs to be regulated at european level, helping to find a solution for informing workers, in order to reduce the number of redundancies and manage restructuring processes through other mechanisms.
in writing. − although national laws on employers' responsibilities towards employees differ considerably in terms of restructuring, this resolution calls for a common set of rules to be found, to the benefit of workers. that's why i gave a final yes vote. i think we need better protection for employees, especially in times of economic crisis. in this respect, i support the idea of transmitting the restructuring decision as many months as possible before it takes effect and of providing retraining courses for employees.
in writing. − i believe that measures taken at european level to prevent such disastrous situations for both workers and employers must be sound and limit the impact of restructuring as much as possible, so that dismissals are not used as a last resort and only after all possible ways of supporting the workers concerned have been explored.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the report on informing and consulting workers, anticipating and managing restructuring, as i believe that a european legal instrument is needed to lay down concrete rules on social dialogue, the social responsibility of employers and informing workers when a restructuring process is necessary. the report's 14 recommendations are essential to ensure that restructuring, which is increasingly taking place across the european union, is carried out with the involvement and prior information of workers. it is also important that restructuring does not only lead to mass redundancies but also to assist workers in reintegrating into the labour market. to this end, it is also important that available european funds, including the european social fund and the globalisation adjustment fund, are accessed and used in a way that effectively contributes to socially and economically responsible restructuring processes.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the resolution containing recommendations to the commission on informing and consulting workers, anticipating and managing restructuring. parliament called on the commission to submit as soon as possible, on the basis of article 225 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union and after consulting the social partners, a proposal for a legal act on the information and consultation of workers, anticipation and management of restructuring. the european parliament also calls on the commission to examine whether measures are needed at union level to supervise the activities of undertakings in order to avoid any abuse that would cause harm, in particular to workers. they argue that when the need for restructuring arises, companies should consider redundancies only as a last resort and only after considering all alternative options and identifying and implementing support measures, if appropriate. i voted for the recommendation that existing financial support schemes, channelled through the european regional development fund (erdf) or the european social fund (esf) under the new financial perspective 2014-2020, should not replace national incentives based on anticipation, preparation and responsible management. i also supported the continuation of the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) with a strengthened capacity to act reactively, temporarily and palliatively.

president-in-office of the council. − madam president, since this is the first occasion at which i have had the honour and great pleasure to address the plenary session of the parliament, allow me to say how much i am looking forward to working with you all over the next six months. i am confident that through good cooperation and indeed a spirit of trust and confidence council and parliament can deliver the results which i think europe’s citizens expect from their institutions. this afternoon’s debate concerns the agreement reached on the credit ratings agency package as you know and let me from the outset express our sincere thanks to the rapporteur, from whom we have just heard, mr domenici, and the shadow rapporteurs for the excellent work which they have put into this file. i would also like to thank sharon bowles as chair of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, as well as to particularly pay tribute to my cypriot colleagues who have worked hard to bring this dossier to a successful conclusion in november last year. this legislative package will be another step towards better regulation of the financial services industry. credit ratings agencies are a very specific sector, and this set of amendments to the existing european legislative framework is an important development, especially in the current circumstances. it is also a logical continuation of the work carried out in 2011, when the credit ratings regulation was first amended in order to bring the credit ratings agencies under the supervision of the european securities and markets authority. the agreement reached towards the end of last year contains a number of very important elements: firstly, there will be a reduction in the role cras play in sovereign risk ratings. unsolicited sovereign ratings will have to be issued in accordance with a calendar and up to three times a year. in order to ensure better investor protection, we have agreed on a minimum european standard, so that where there have been cases of intentional or negligent infringement of the law by cras, investors will be entitled to compensation for damages if investment decisions have been negatively influenced as a result. competition will be increased in a market which has to date been dominated by a small number of very large cras. this will require us to test the regime of mandatory rotation of agencies, initially only affecting a limited range of instruments, but with the possibility of extending these to cover a wider range of instruments in due course. transparency regarding structured finance instruments will increase. for example, issuers will be required to engage at least two different credit rating agencies to rate such instruments. furthermore, there will be greater disclosure of information about underlying assets and this should increase the number of unsolicited ratings and so increase competition. where there is a risk of conflict of interest, disclosure rules on shareholdings will be enhanced. the size of direct and indirect shareholdings in cras will be limited. we all know that the ‘issuer pays’ model has some flaws, and that relationships between the shareholders of credit rating agencies and the rated entities risk creating conflicts of interest. this was not adequately addressed under the existing rules and we have therefore agreed to strengthen the independence of cras. we have also reduced excessive reliance on credit ratings in the markets. we have agreed on safeguards that will prevent financial instruments from relying solely or too mechanically on credit ratings when they take investment decisions. the work on reducing over-reliance on credit ratings in the european law will continue. the council considers that this new regulation constitutes a very serious step in that direction and in the development of a wider range of alternatives to credit ratings. we are also convinced that we are making good progress in achieving greater competition in the credit ratings sector over the medium term. in our view, the text agreed towards the end of last year constitutes a very good balance. it is the product of hard work by all concerned, and an excellent level of cooperation between our two institutions. i commend the outcome to this house, and very much hope that it will secure strong support when you vote on it tomorrow.
member of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, mr rapporteur, madam minister, we are going to take a further, necessary step together in this great movement which wants, together with you, and as the g20 has wished, that every financial actor - and we are talking about many major financial actors with the rating agency - every sector, every product should be subject to public regulation as soon as possible, and this in order to put all these actors, products and sectors at the service of the real economy, of business and employment. our determination is intact and must remain intact, to draw all the lessons from the crises which are, as we well know, successive but also interconnected with each other, and it is in this spirit that we have brought together initial responses over the last two years. this is particularly true, ladies and gentlemen, of the credit rating agencies, to which we had to be as responsive as possible. i share the view of your rapporteur, mr domenici, on this point. these agencies may have contributed to market volatility and speculation. i want to thank the european parliament for its work, for the speed of its work and for the intensive cooperation we have had on all these new legislative initiatives. we haven't finished our work; i am therefore saying to lucinda creighton: i thank the irish presidency. we were able to verify last thursday his determination to go ahead with all the other texts which are now on your table and that of the ministers. i would also like to thank your rapporteur, mr domenici, the fictitious rapporteurs, jean-paul gauzès, sven giegold, wolf klinz, ashley fox, and all those who worked on this text, for their commitment and the dynamic compromise we have reached since the presentation of the commission's proposal. i would like to stress six points which have just been mentioned by the presidency and lucinda creighton. first, the timetable for the rating of sovereign debt. i am particularly pleased with the compromise reached on the framework for the rating of sovereign debts. we all remember some unfortunate events that have taken place in the past year. we want to put an end to the risks of disorganization, of destabilizing the markets, by regulating the sometimes untimely publication of sovereign ratings. the rating agencies will now be required to establish an annual rating schedule, which will include a maximum of three unsolicited sovereign debt ratings. these ratings shall be published on the friday after the close of trading and at least one hour before the opening of trading. finally, the sovereign debt rating will be done in a transparent manner. again, this is a key word for all our proposals. governments, like investors, will have access to the elements on which the rating is based. second, reduce the reliance on external ratings. the new framework you are about to approve will reduce and ultimately eliminate the over-reliance on credit ratings. in practice, financial institutions will no longer be able to rely exclusively, and sometimes blindly, on credit ratings for their investments. they will have to revise their internal rules to eliminate references to ratings where they may have - and sometimes have had - mechanical effects. the commission will assess the market situation before the end of 2015, in particular the existence of alternatives to credit ratings. can we go further, eliminate all references to external ratings by 2020, if there are enough alternatives available? in any case, we will - i will - work on this with the same willingness. thirdly, the protection of investors and issuers, with a civil liability regime, which is introduced by compromise, at the level of the whole european union. this is an essential measure in view of the impact that the rating can have both on the rated party - the issuer or the state - and on investors, markets and the european economy in general. from now on, rating agencies can be held accountable for their mistakes, which is the least of it, when it comes to gross negligence or intentional violations of the law. this is a major step forward for investor protection and issuer protection. we're going to make the rating agencies more accountable for what they do. fourthly, the limitation of shareholding. we know that the composition of shareholders and the holdings of rating agencies can be a source of conflicts of interest. it's a risk that's not theoretical. it can have a negative effect on the quality of the rating. for this reason, the regulation provides for transparency requirements, but also for formal limitations on the composition of the shareholders. in order to ensure the independence of the agencies and proper risk assessment, an obligation of transparency is established; it applies in several situations: where the agency has an interest in the rated entity or its products; where the rated entity is a shareholder of the agency; or where the agency's shareholders have an interest in the rated entity or its products. such a transparency obligation will be imposed on shareholders exceeding 5% of the capital of an agency and, beyond the 10% threshold, there will be a ban on listing. in addition, the participation of the same investor in several agencies is limited to a threshold of 5% per agency. fifth, the opening up of the rating market. to introduce more competition - i was committed to this - in the event of multiple ratings, issuers are encouraged to use at least one smaller rating agency, following the 'apply or explain' principle. a four-year rollover obligation is also introduced for a certain form of structured products, namely retitling. this measure is, in my view, a first test. it will be evaluated by the commission, which will submit it to you, and which may, if necessary, lead to an extension of the scope of the principle of rotation. finally, the sixth point, the european rating platform, which i know many of you are very fond of. the ratings will be published on a european rating platform. this measure will enhance the visibility and comparability of ratings of financial instruments and will help investors, in particular, to carry out their own solvency assessment. in addition, due to the complexity of structured finance instruments and their role in the financial crisis, the draft regulation requires issuers of structured products to publish more data on the performance of underlying assets. in response to the request of the european parliament, the commission will present, by the end of 2016, a report to the european parliament and the council, based on market developments, on the merits of a possible european credit rating agency dedicated to the assessment of the solvency of member states and their sovereign debt. the commission will also consider the alternative idea of a european credit rating foundation for corporate ratings and structured finance products. ladies and gentlemen, as your rapporteur has said and as the presidency has stressed, the new legislative framework, which complements the previous texts we have implemented together on credit rating agencies, is in line with a commitment made by europe in the context of the g20. it proposes a set of complementary measures - which i believe are effective - which will lead to one of our objectives, namely to strengthen the transparency and stability of financial markets. i thank you not only for your attention but also for the part your parliament has played in the preparation of this text and in the improvement of its content.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on legal affairs. − as the shadow rapporteur of the epp group, i agreed with the other rapporteurs, including the lead rapporteur for the opinion, that our committee's opinion should focus on one aspect of the commission's proposal for a regulation, namely civil liability. although our committee could make amendments to any article in the commission's proposal, and although it was merely an opinion to the committee responsible for the subject-matter, in the econ case, we decided by common accord to drop all other amendments, both we, the rapporteurs, and the other members of our committee, except for the amendment on civil liability. the reason why we took such a decision, a decision communicated to the econ commission, was to concentrate all our concern and competence towards a 100% legal aspect and which, normally, should have been in the competence of the juri, as the main committee. but since the subject of the commission's proposal is the regulation of financial institutions, the committee responsible is econ and we respect that rule. so our committee has, as i said, dropped the amendment on issues of external rotation of credit rating agencies, shareholder structure or conflict of interest, even though at least the last two issues would have been in our area of competence if credit rating agencies were not considered financial institutions. as far as civil liability is concerned, our committee has found that a reversal of the burden of proof is a proposal at least legally uninspired, being in contradiction with the principle preserved in roman law itself: whoever makes a claim must prove it. our committee has further argued that there are other reasons why a reversal of the burden of proof is unfortunate. unfortunately, the econ committee did not agree with the juri committee's opinion, although it focused on one aspect, as i said. of course, formally, it is the right of the econ commission to take elements from a committee's opinion for its opinion or not. finally, i would like to welcome the outcome of the trialogue, which has returned to the traditional form of civil liability in terms of burden of proof.
the credit ratings published by the agencies are no longer just opinions. they have significant consequences for the well-being of a nation, having the capacity to worsen considerably the financial situation of a state. some eu member states are now in a vicious circle: they are facing debt repayment difficulties as a result of ratings agencies' assessments, while confirming their forecasts. the agencies are not afraid to make policy recommendations, putting pressure on government decisions. these institutions, characterised by a lack of transparency and conflicts of interest, have often published erroneous assessments. by 2007, they rated the toxic assets held by u.s. banks as risk-free, and soon, the global financial crisis was caused by these types of assets. in this context, i would like to welcome the present agreement on credit rating agencies, which will establish clear rules in this area, freeing member states from their dependence on these institutions. the fixed timing of the country rating will no longer allow for the publication of short-term ratings ahead of major political events with the aim of influencing them. the agencies will also no longer be able to issue policy recommendations. the commission's assessment of the possibility of setting up a european public rating agency will also be welcomed. finally, i would like to congratulate mr domenici on this excellent report.
credit rating agencies play a particularly important role in influencing the behaviour of economic and financial operators and there have been many cases where the lack of objectivity and transparency of external credit rating agencies has led to sharp falls in european credit ratings and contagion across the european union. i therefore believe that, in order to eliminate the suspicions and negative effects generated by these institutions, there is an urgent need to publish the full research reports accompanying the rating and to develop a tool for comparing the ratings by promoting common standards for rating grades and the existence of a single european rating index. furthermore, in order to hold those agencies accountable and to limit their abusive decision-making, i consider that users who suffer losses due to an inaccurate rating published by a credit rating agency should have adequate remedies to take action against such abuses.
both the proposals in mr pallone's report and the actual situation in the member states support our conclusion that they are on the right track. many tough measures have been taken by member states to eliminate excessive deficits. today, the european union is better equipped with the tools it needs to enable member states to manage their public finances in a sustainable way in the future. i would like to stress in particular the importance of the european semester, an instrument which is proving ever more useful and effective. solidarity at the level of the european union has played a big part in the financial and budgetary recovery of some member states, but what it has finally shown us is that the responsibility of each member state for its public finances cannot be avoided. in conclusion, i would like to express my concern that while tens of millions of citizens in the member states have suffered the consequences of harsh austerity measures, international companies and citizens continue to evade tax revenues in the member states by using tax havens and here we are still waiting for initiatives from the european commission.
article 107 (3) (e) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union provides that other categories of state aid considered compatible with the internal market are to be determined by a decision of the council acting on a proposal from the commission. the commission stated in its communication of may 2012 on state aid modernisation that it would engage in an open dialogue with the european parliament and other stakeholders with a view to a debate on legislative proposals to modernise state aid. we stress that the revision and simplification of the state aid guidelines must be done with the involvement of the european parliament. should the commission decide to extend the scope and coverage of aid measures exempted from the ex ante notification requirement, member states will have more responsibilities in ensuring the correct application of state aid rules. the state aid procedure should also be simplified as regards the handling of complaints.
the commission has repeatedly stated its intention to amend, at the end of 2012 or the beginning of 2013, directive 96/53 laying down, for certain road vehicles circulating within the community, the maximum authorised dimensions in national and international traffic and the maximum authorised weight in international traffic. obviously, parliament must have an important say in these amendments. the parliament and the council are currently working on amending regulation 3821/85/ec on digital tachographs. parliament called, by a large majority, for the introduction of the weight sensor at first reading. parliament believes that its introduction will provide useful information on loading and unloading operations. in the negotiations with the council of the european union, the commission representatives informed us that the weight sensor would be introduced in the context of the expected amendment of directive 96/53/ec. commissioner, i would like to ask you directly whether the amendment to directive 96/53/ec also envisages the introduction of the weight sensor.

in writing. as the irish presidency's programme papers show, the european union must focus not only on taking measures to ensure the economic and institutional stability of the member states, but also on translating these measures into real benefits for european citizens. despite the stabilising effect of several governance measures adopted in recent years, european citizens continue to face the obvious problem of falling incomes or the dire prospects of long-term unemployment. i therefore support the irish presidency's policy of putting european citizens at the centre of future political efforts. i also believe it is important that the european union continues to take as assertive a political leadership position as possible in combating the effects of climate change. it is important, however, that at this level the imperative of reducing greenhouse gas emissions is not only the subject of dedicated efforts by the european union but also of a broad coordination of all union policies that have an impact at this level.
in writing. with ireland taking over the presidency of the european union, the focus is on the measures that will need to be taken in the coming period to get the european economy back on track by promoting growth and job creation. ireland will need to drive forward the implementation of the jobs and growth pact, a package of measures on fiscal consolidation, reducing unemployment, international trade and other areas that can create jobs and growth. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the right to leave for maternity leave. there are member states that have expressed concern about the changes and costs associated with this leave. according to four member states (germany, the uk, ireland and the czech republic), the changes introduced by the ep have made it very difficult to reach a common position in the council. the irish presidency could therefore play a key role in the negotiations to unlock the current situation. the european council also stressed the importance of the eu's role in the international community, and called on the eu to continue to play a leading role in the international community.
in writing. i would first like to welcome the irish presidency of the european union and express my hope that it will be able to carry out a large part of the programme drawn up for the next six months. economic recovery and job creation, especially for young people, are among the ambitious goals, the achievement of which corresponds to the expectations of european citizens. however, i cannot help but regret that one of the central points of all the countries that have held the eu presidency since the beginning of 2011 - the accession of romania and bulgaria to the schengen area - is not among ireland's priorities. mrs lucinda creighton recently said that the irish presidency would not deal with 'small' issues and recalled that ireland is one of the long-standing members of the eu. that is why i am advocating that romania's accession to schengen be included in the list of priorities, given that the free movement of goods, capital and people would make an important contribution to the objective of economic growth. neglecting this important aspect for my country would validate the arguments that make schengen an 'exclusive club', eroding the fundamental freedoms on which the european union is based.
in writing. it is important that the new irish presidency has included both the accession of romania and bulgaria to the schengen area and schengen reform among its priorities. now that the new romanian government, led by victor ponta, has as its first european policy priority the admission of romania to the schengen area and presents clear political guarantees, the irish presidency has the opportunity to redress the injustice perpetrated since 2011 and which led to the postponement of accession on criteria totally foreign to the letter and spirit of the treaties. it is widely accepted that both countries have been preparing for almost two years to become members of the schengen area, and on some components of the acquis, such as border control infrastructure, they are the best performing countries in the whole of europe. as regards the schengen package, we are at a stage of negotiations where the difference between a final agreement and a failure of the negotiations depends strictly on the political will of the member states to move towards a truly european system of managing schengen. the irish presidency thus has a choice between being recognised as having helped to consolidate one of the greatest achievements in the history of the eu or, on the contrary, as having contributed to the dismantling of schengen.

in writing. − i voted in favour of amending the calendar of parliament's sessions for 2013 because i believe that the decision of the european court of justice must be respected. the court has decided that there must be 12 plenary sessions a year, all of which must take place in strasbourg. these plenary sessions will also have to last four days. in 2011, parliament amended the calendar of sittings for 2012 and 2013, uniting two plenary sessions in a single week. thus, the duration of these two sessions was reduced to only two days. in rejecting this decision, the court of justice of the european union ordered parliament to change the calendar of plenary sessions for 2013.
in writing. − i would like to mention that i voted against the calendar of plenary sessions for 2013 and that i am not in favour of travelling to strasbourg every month, as this would involve spending very large sums of money, which could represent significant savings for the union budget.
in writing. − i voted for the revised calendar for 2013, in the spirit of respecting the decision of the european court of justice. however, in the current context of economic crisis, the european parliament should also reduce its spending. the fact that meps, assistants and european officials are obliged to travel to strasbourg once a month for the plenary session costs the european parliament some €180 million a year. add to that a consumption of 19,000 tons of co2. i believe that the european parliament should have the right to decide on its own organisation and to choose, accordingly, a single location for its work. heads of state and government must respect the will of the majority - 75% of meps voted in 2012 in favour of choosing a single seat for the ep - and revise the european treaty.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the internal organisation decision as regards the amendment of the european parliament's calendar of plenary sessions - 2013. this vote on the timetable for plenary meetings to be held in strasbourg is in line with the decision of the european court of justice of december 2012 (case c-237/11). according to the court's decision and the vote in the european parliament, all plenary sessions of the parliament must be held in strasbourg (eastern france) and cannot be split in favour of brussels. the court thus annulled a vote by the european parliament which decided to split the october 2012 and 2013 plenary sessions in order to limit the time of presence of meps in strasbourg. the treaties require the european parliament, which has its seat in strasbourg, to meet in plenary sessions 12 times a year. normally, two plenary sessions are held in strasbourg in the autumn in the same month to compensate for the absence of a plenary session in august. for 2013, these two plenary sessions will take place in october.
