the reporter. − i would like to answer very briefly to a few concerns, all related to the access of the research authorities to the eurodac database on the basis of yes or you do not have this fingerprint in the eurodac database. and currently, member states have access to the fingerprints of asylum seekers or those found illegally in the european union, based on bilateral cooperation, but what we've done with this eurodac is we've shortened the time it takes you to get this information. so instead of asking 26 member states to send the fingerprint found at the crime scene, you now ask eurodac. basically, i just cut down on the reaction time. why are we doing this? let's find the balance, because the balance is the essence of reconciling all interests; namely to find any suspects, any victims or any witnesses to a terrorist crime or a serious crime. we also have a lot of safeguards: no application can be sent to eurodac until it has been verified by certain institutions designated in advance by the authorities of each member state. there are also very strict criteria on whether or not you can ask eurodac for this information. we have designated authorities with the application, we have designated authorities to verify the application and then it's sent, plus the criteria on which it can be sent and they're restrictive. and i would also point out that when these fingerprints are collected, the individuals are informed that they may be used for this purpose. and one last thing: we all know that we require biometric passports from candidate countries and those who want visa liberalisation, and you should know that all these biometric passports also involve fingerprinting. in romania it's the same; for example, last week they took my fingerprint when i applied for a biometric passport. i don't feel discriminated against, we don't discriminate against anyone, we just use these databases in the case of serious crimes.
rapporteur. − mr president, colleagues, each year a survey is carried out on how european citizens see the european union. each and every time, more than 50 % say that the biggest achievement of the eu is free movement. there are good reasons for this answer. in a europe where for decades people, even families, were separated by borders and horrendous controls, finding ourselves all together in an area where movement is free gives us the feeling of living in one big house. it is also very easy to notice the economic benefits for our businesses. then why hesitate for more than a year and a half to reach an agreement on something so much wanted and appreciated by european citizens? the answer is as simple as it is complicated. a populist approach has taken over several eu member states and the ongoing elections here and there have determined a switch in the approach of some governments – but here we are. the text on the schengen border code, for which i am the rapporteur, sets clear rules and checks and balances for last-resort situations involving the introduction of border controls at internal borders, to avoid any misuse or abuse. i admit i would have loved a 100 % community decision on the reintroduction of border controls, but apparently that time has not yet come. however, it is fair to say that we succeeded in introducing a degree of community dimension and additional guarantees to ensure that the mechanism would not be misused. the current possibilities for reintroducing border controls have been clarified, and among the safeguards we should note a proportionality test of the impact of the measures and, where appropriate, consultations and meetings among the member states affected by the reintroduction of border controls, and opinions by the commission. a new option of reintroducing border controls, which was in fact the request, or rather the demand, addressed by the council to the commission two years ago, will be used only as a last resort in exceptional circumstances, as a result of persistent, serious deficiencies related to external border controls. but, in that case, the proposal will come from the commission after thorough evaluation. among other additional checks and balances, we should mention that a recital was introduced so as to keep our 2011 commitment. migration and the crossing of external borders by a large number of third country nationals should not per se be considered to be a threat to public policy or to internal security. the total period during which border controls are reintroduced on the basis of a serious threat to public policy or internal security cannot exceed two months. the commission will present to the european parliament and the council, at least annually, a report on the functioning of the area without internal border controls. this report is to include a list of all decisions to reintroduce internal border controls taken during the relevant year. i would like to say a few words also on mr coelho’s report, for which i am a shadow. the true achievement here is the role of the commission. if today it is a mere observer and the mechanism is based on a peer-to-peer review, in future the commission will be responsible for most decisions to be taken either in comitology, in cooperation with member states, or acting alone. the council can adopt recommendations only upon proposals from the commission. it is also interesting to note that in relation to the decision-making process, a joint statement from the three institutions has been adopted, and it provides that any future commission proposal amending the evaluation mechanism should be submitted to parliament for consultation. if adopted – and i hope it will be adopted – it will set a precedent, as it interprets article 70, whereby parliament should only be informed in a creative way, namely a commitment to consult.
on behalf of the s&d group. first of all, i would like to congratulate the two rapporteurs on the work and tenacity they have shown over the past two years to get to this point. i want to start by saying that this agreement on schengen governance is relatively far from what the european commission proposed two years ago; however, i believe it represents progress compared to the situation so far. the old model of intergovernmental governance has given rise to abuses and restrictions of freedom of movement within schengen. we have to keep in mind that these abuses are probably just the tip of the iceberg, and that many other issues in border management have simply been ignored because of the friendly way of evaluating. i would add that, up to now, there have been two assessment systems: one very relaxed and applicable to all schengen states and another, more stringent, for the candidate countries. this double standard, and the intergovernmental governance, has led to the absurd situation that some candidate countries, such as romania and bulgaria, are denied access to schengen, even though it is widely accepted that these two countries apply the highest standards of border management in the european union. the new agreement brings considerable improvements, as the same rules will apply to all and the evaluation process will be europeanised even more efficiently. the european commission will play a central role in the new schengen governance, as it will coordinate the entire evaluation process and have a say in the possible reintroduction of internal border controls. the new evaluation mechanism will be based on objective data and frontex risk analysis and will allow for unannounced visits, including at internal borders, which have not been possible until now. from now on, there will be a follow-up plan, coordinated by the european commission, whenever weaknesses in the application of the acquis are identified. this means firstly support and assistance measures, but also a deterrent system, whereby the commission can propose the temporary reintroduction of internal border controls in the event of very serious and persistent deficiencies. at the same time, the european parliament will play a much more important role, by having access to all the data and overseeing the entire evaluation process and being consulted in case of changes to the mechanism. in conclusion, i would like to stress that for my country and for the other member states outside the schengen area, all this will not be enough if the europeanisation of governance is not also applied to the way in which new members are admitted to the schengen area. this is all the more evident as the accession of romania and bulgaria has been blocked for more than two years, for reasons that have nothing to do with the rules and the european spirit of good cooperation. that is why i am planning to propose to parliament for debate a new possible european way of accepting new schengen members and i hope i can count on your support.
mr president, i will speak again at the end. but i can take advantage of this and thank the irish presidency very much, since the minister will have to leave. yes, minister, i thank you deeply for all your efforts in coming to the conclusion of this report.
i support the three reports in the schengen package because they defend the right to free movement within the european union, one of the most precious assets the union has. i'd like to mention some of the improvements brought about by these reports. 1 - the standards for schengen member states are more relaxed than for candidate countries such as romania and bulgaria. through these reports, the standards are made equal for everyone: for the candidate countries as well as for the member states, that is, the standards will also be raised in the schengen countries that are already members. secondly, monitoring of internal border controls, monitoring of illegal internal border controls will be possible, which is not possible today. for example, teams of experts can board buses carrying tourists from different countries to other eu countries and see for themselves whether or not these people are subject to illegal checks. a third improvement is that the possibility of reintroducing border controls can be made much more restrictive than before, namely only with the agreement of the european commission, and the decision is taken by the council of the union, with the approval of the european commission. again, based on well-established criteria and solely to protect public order. so all of this will lead to transport, to travel, to free movement in the european union on an equal basis for all citizens.
it is gratifying that these two regulations aim to improve the schengen evaluation mechanism to address crisis situations in the common regions, especially at the borders of the countries of the european union. however, it is worrying that nothing is being done at european level to resolve the issue of bulgaria and romania's accession to the schengen area. the persistence of opposition by certain member states is an abuse which runs counter to the long-term principles and objectives of the european union. the position of these states has shown, once again, that although all member states enjoy common responsibilities, unfortunately some states do not enjoy the same benefits. ladies and gentlemen, these populist ambitions will only weaken the power of the european union and reduce our credibility globally. given that all the conditions for accession have been met, i hereby call on all the institutions responsible to identify and propose for implementation all the necessary measures to contribute to the successful enlargement of the schengen area and to eliminate this injustice.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, thank you very much, first of all, to mr sánchez presedo for this excellent report on the 2011 annual competition report. and my thanks also to those members from the committee on employment and social affairs (econ), the committee on the internal market and consumer protection (imco) and the committee on transport and tourism (tran) – mr ungureanu, mr schwab and mr kamall – who also contributed to parliament’s report on our work in 2011. this is the fourth competition report during the term in office of the barroso ii commission, of my term in office as commissioner for competition, and i am happy to say before this parliament that the dialogue between our two institutions on competition policy continues to deepen and i welcome very much your support for the work of the commission on competition enforcement. as you know, this report was structured to better respond to parliament’s wishes, allowing us to focus on key policy areas. we have continued to improve the report in 2012. i had the opportunity recently to present this new report to the econ committee and i hope that we have been able to reflect some of your comments on last year’s report in this year’s one. as i said when i presented the 2011 report to you, almost one year ago, one of our main goals is to maintain stability amid persistent turbulence in financial markets. we continue to use state aid rules to restructure and resolve banks which needed public support to preserve financial stability, minimise the cost to public finances, and ensure that restructured banks are sufficiently viable to be able to lend to companies and households. on this point i fully agree with mr sánchez presedo’s words a few minutes ago. you are well aware of the ongoing discussions around banking supervision and restructuring. on the competition side, we will soon put forward revised state aid guidelines for banks. they will reflect current practice in our case work and include stricter burden-sharing requirements for shareholders and junior creditors, and will provide that, in principle, only reversible measures – like loans or guarantees – can be approved as rescue aid. thus, we hope that taxpayers will feel less of the pain when a bank needs to be restructured. one year ago i outlined our plans for the modernisation of state aid. since then we have been working hard to take this forward, and i welcome the contribution of the econ committee and the transport committee to this work through the pietikäinen and the dorfmann reports. i look forward to these reports being adopted in this parliament in due course. another important project has been the revision of the regional aid guidelines, which was discussed here last night based on the vlasák report and which the commission will try to adopt in the coming weeks. i welcome parliament’s support for our firm enforcement of the antitrust rules and for the ongoing fight against cartels, in which both our fining policy and settlement procedure play important roles. i note your reiterated call for the commission to review the fining guidelines. this is a topic which we have discussed on several occasions during recent years. i want to repeat that setting the fines is not an arbitrary exercise. the framework for our fining powers and fining policy is set out in a council regulation – regulation (ec) no 1/2003. this contains objective criteria which limit our discretion: the fines shall reflect the gravity and the duration of the infringements and cannot exceed 10 % of the undertaking’s total worldwide turnover. we also decided, as have other competition authorities, and as a matter of transparency, to provide further details of our methodology in the guidelines – the guidelines that are binding for our work. these guidelines take the view that the current legal framework ensures that fines achieve punitive and deterrent effects while allowing the commission to react quickly to and take into account company-specific and market-related situations. the european court of justice has confirmed the legality of this approach on several occasions. in your report, parliament draws the commission’s attention to several specific sectoral issues. we share your concerns about the level of competition in sectors such as energy and transport. in such fields, our policy and our regulatory work go hand in hand. concerning the full implementation of the third energy package, my colleague mr oettinger and his directorate-general may take the lead; the same in the transport sector with my colleague mr kallas and the same in the digital sector, in the telecoms sector, with my colleague ms neelie kroes. as you said, in difficult times it is ever more important for markets to work efficiently and fairly, to deliver the benefits to businesses of all sizes and to european citizens and consumers, and with your help, we will continue to achieve this. in another area of key importance to consumers, the commission shares your concerns in relation to the volatility of food prices. the report published by the european competition network last year shows that the food sector has been a priority for competition authorities, which have been very active in enforcing competition law and monitoring market developments. between 2001 and 2011, the national competition authorities investigated more than 180 antitrust cases in this area, took close to 1 300 merger decisions, and monitored around 100 activities. the commission stands ready to investigate any possible anti-competitive agreements between different players in the supply chain which would ultimately lead to price increases for our consumers. i also agree fully with you that consumers are the final beneficiaries of our competition enforcement action. so i think that on all these areas we probably share the same objectives, the same priorities, and i hope very much that we will continue i particularly appreciate the flexibility of the european commission in adapting competition and state aid policy to the new challenges posed by the financial and economic crisis. i would also like to thank commissioner almunia for the openness and transparency in the structured dialogue with the members of the econ committee. i would like to stress, however, the persistence of the large price differences which still exist for some products and services between the different member states within the single market. it demonstrates that there are still obstacles to competition in this single market and it is the european commission's duty to identify these obstacles and to act to remove them for the benefit of competition and european citizens.
in writing. competition is the cornerstone of the internal market and an important driver of economic development and the well-being of european consumers, as has been confirmed over time. the economic crisis we are experiencing has re-ignited some protectionist tendencies and fuelled anti-competitive discourse. i believe that the european institutions should counter these trends by putting more emphasis on the benefits of competition for consumers in particular, in order to increase the legitimacy of competition policy. i would like to congratulate the commission on the way it has implemented competition policy in 2011. however, i believe that there are certain aspects that deserve a little more attention in the future, especially from the consumer's point of view. these include the full implementation of the energy package, which is of major importance to european consumers in the context of rising energy prices, the close monitoring of competition in the agri-food sector or the move towards a more open market for electronic payments. i conclude by stressing once again the importance for consumers of alternative dispute resolution and collective actions for damages for damage caused by non-compliance with competition rules.
this report aims at aligning with the provisions of the lisbon treaty and the commission is calling for a whole range of powers relating to illegal fishing to be conferred under the treaty. of course, these powers should be conferred on the commission to enable it to implement the legislation. but i ask the commission to exercise these powers effectively and efficiently in combating illegal fishing. in recent years, poaching has taken on unprecedented proportions in the black sea. last year, the romanian authorities seized 120 poaching vessels, most of them turkish or ukrainian, so from countries outside the union or not subject to strict european rules. i would remind the commission that a large part of the shortcomings in the management of fisheries in the black sea are linked to the lack of a regional organisation for this area and the establishment of a black sea committee is a repeated request of this parliament.

in writing. – 22.8% of young people in the eu are currently unemployed, with youth unemployment exceeding 50% in some member states. 8.3 million europeans under 25 years and an additional 6.5 million young people aged 25–29 are neither in employment nor in education or training. we should start to work on the creation of automatic stabilisers at the eu level, starting with the youth guarantee schemes, which should be accompanied by a quality framework in order to ensure that the education, training and jobs offered include appropriate pay, working conditions and health and safety standards. the member states should improve cooperation between businesses and the educational sector at all levels, with a scope of better linking curricula to the demands of the labour market, more flexible curricula are needed in order to better adapt to future labour market developments. social investment can go hand in hand with efficient incentives, such as employment subsidies or insurance contributions for young people that will guarantee decent living and working conditions, in order to encourage public and private employers to hire young people, invest in both quality job creation for young people and continuous training and upgrading of their skills during employment, and support entrepreneurship among youth.
in writing. it is clear that the european project has reached a major impasse. the eu was seen as an alternative model of globalisation, precisely because of the social aspects of the project. now, instead of looking at the causes of our situation, we're looking for the culprits. the elements that were supposed to unite us - the single currency, eu enlargement, the movement of labour - have become the causes of their division. i think the key issue is the historical development gaps between different parts of the continent, which the crisis has brought to the fore and which austerity is exacerbating. without a consistent and systematic effort to reduce the development gap, the problems we are talking about now will get worse. the relaunch of the european project should begin with deepening political integration. it would be the first sign that the need to reduce the democratic deficit and involve citizens in decisions affecting them is understood, including by increasing the powers of the european parliament, which truly exercises the sovereignty of european citizens.
in writing. the reintroduction of the debate on job creation, with a focus on youth, on the council's agenda, once again shows the alarming situation of young europeans. that is why we need structural reforms at national and community level more than ever to create jobs focused on the young workforce. these efforts should be directed towards: matching community employment strategies to the future needs of the european economy, reducing the tax burden on companies employing young people under 30, and programmes to support the development of entrepreneurship among young people through the creation of special business incubators for young people, increased access to european funds and business advice.
in writing. the june european council will focus on economic policy, addressing three main issues: the conclusion of this year's european semester (coordination of member states' economic and fiscal policies), including country-specific recommendations; the assessment of efforts to boost competitiveness, jobs and growth, with a focus on initiatives to improve youth employment and finance the economy; progress in completing the eu's economic and monetary union, in particular the banking union. we ask the council to focus on boosting competitiveness, jobs and growth. the eu must develop an industrial policy capable of rebuilding european industry in an eco-efficient manner. the eu's industrial development must be accompanied by measures to finance the european economy, so as to ensure both jobs in the eu and the eu's global competitiveness. finally, i believe that the eu must invest in preserving the european social model. without investment in education and health, in decent jobs and in guaranteeing a decent pension, the eu has no future. the eu's most important asset is its 500 million citizens, and it is therefore time for the eu to invest in their present and future.
