in writing. − the average age of a ship sent for recycling has varied over time from 26 years in the 1990s to 32 during the financial boom of the mid-2000s, but it is very likely to decline again significantly as a result of the enormous overcapacity and economic crisis. proper ship recycling requires the development of a ship recycling plan based on a correct inventory. such a plan should be approved by the competent authorities. i believe that additional provisions are needed to ensure that recycling and waste treatment are carried out in environmentally safe conditions.
in writing. − the predominant method of dismantling ships through so-called 'deliberate failure' is not a safe and correct method of recycling. ship recycling facilities with low or no standards for the protection of workers, human health and the environment offer the most attractive price for waste vessels. as a result, the vast majority of the world's fleet of ships sent for recycling are dismantled on the beaches of certain countries in human degrading and environmentally hazardous conditions. the european parliament today strongly opposed the extremely dangerous and polluting practices of such a method and believes that we must ensure that old ships under the european flag are only recycled in eu-approved facilities and standards. the establishment of a european list of ship recycling facilities will contribute to the objective of safe and environmentally sound recycling and to better enforcement by facilitating flag state control of ships sent for recycling. the requirements applicable to ship recycling facilities should be based on the hong kong convention but should be broader in order to achieve a level of protection of human health and the environment broadly equivalent to that in the union.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report, which aims to impose european standards for the dismantling of ships flying the flag of a member state of the european union. the regulation will require the dismantling of these vessels at yards that meet new environmental and social standards. this is a very positive development and i am pleased with the positive result of the vote on this text, which had previously been agreed between parliament and the member states. it should come into force within two to five years, time for a sufficient number of companies to comply with the standards. this text is a fundamental step forward. end-of-life ships can pose a significant danger and as such should only be dismantled within an oecd country, according to a 1998 regulation. more than 90% of them will die outside the oecd area, often in south-east asia, where their dismantling poses a danger to workers. the new rules will require that ships be dismantled in structures designed, built and operated in a safe and environmentally sound manner, which have been approved by the european union.
in writing. − the eu-27 population is in a progressive ageing process. one way of illustrating this structural change in the eu-27 population is the demographic dependency ratio, which analyses the relationship between the number of elderly people (aged 65 or over) and the working-age population (15-64 years). the population aged 65 and over was equivalent to 25.9% of the working-age population in the eu-27 as of the beginning of 2010. demographic issues are multiplying and playing an increasingly important role in the development of the eu. only when statistical data are available can relevant comparisons be made from which conclusions and directions for action can be drawn. i therefore believe that harmonisation of demographic statistics at european level is necessary to make it easier to compare data.
in writing. − this proposal aims to regulate the provision and harmonisation of demographic data in the member states. this implies the creation of a common framework for the systematic production of european demographic statistics, governing the collection, processing and transmission of demographic statistics as well as statistical data on civil status events. due to the increasingly complex demographic challenges, the need for common legislation at european level on demographic statistics has become evident. in almost every policy area in which the eu is active, whether economic, social or environmental, high-quality demographic statistics are needed to help formulate operational objectives and to assess progress, for example, to make valid comparisons between member states. the proposal aims to harmonise the concepts, topics covered and characteristics of the information required, the coverage, the qualitative criteria, the deadlines and the reporting results, with a view to obtaining relevant, timely, comparable and coherent european statistics. the freedom to choose data sources in accordance with national law and principles, together with the possibility to use statistical estimation methods and techniques, should reduce the financial and administrative burden on respondents, national, regional or local authorities and citizens.
in writing. − the use of common european statistical methods should also be applied in the demographic field and i believe that it will be beneficial for europe if the evaluation of data at european level takes into account local, regional and national databases on demographic trends and there is a permanent exchange of good practices between states, regions and localities. i support the commission's proposal to use the data obtained to create indicators of various types, including 'demographic vulnerability indices', to highlight which european regions are most exposed to demographic change.
in writing. - in order to optimise the data on the european population and to have a general picture that is as true and reliable as possible, i voted in favour of mr sógor's report. the operation of this service will be improved by the inclusion and harmonisation of local (regional and national) databases with the previously collected data. demographic studies are now an important analytical tool, essential for the union and the member states, which can effectively study such data, draw conclusions from them and use the results in order to make targeted and effective operational choices.
in writing. − the lack of unity and consistency of statistical data on demographic developments creates problems for the commission in the development of european union policies, such as cohesion policy, and affects its recommendations on employment. demographic trends are of concern in most regions and call attention to the need for demographic policies with long-term results and for broad economic policies that increase birth rates and regional development. regular monitoring of demographic developments, as well as harmonisation of data and assessment of their quality, are essential in an increasingly globalised europe, where demographic transitions have become an integral part of the process of economic and social development. i therefore believe that a common methodology for the collection of demographic data is needed in order to produce uniform statistics at european level, in accordance with the european statistics code of practice. the more reliable the data provided, the faster eu policies will take effect. thank you!
in writing − the european union (eu) needs to keep an accurate and uniform population count according to the criteria defined by international standards, as does the un. it was a draft document of a technical nature, since the data will be used as the basis for qualified majority voting in the council of the european union as from 1 november 2014, in accordance with the treaty of lisbon. in my view, the text of the report, adopted by consensus by the eu institutions and the european parliament (ep) political groups, provides flexibility for member states, as the qualified majority ratio can be determined on the basis of the total population, using scientifically based methods, inter alia, well documented and publicly available. following my suggestion, two new points were incorporated into the text of the document. under these, member states will have feasibility studies carried out and this obligation will not impose a specific financial burden on them, as the union will provide them with support in this area. finally, by means of a review clause, the document guarantees the member states concerned that the adopted statistical method does not create a disadvantage for them: the european commission (ec) is required to carry out a survey every five years and to submit its conclusions to the european parliament (ep) for approval.

in writing. − i voted in support of this report because i agree that the human rights situation in the sahel region is in dire need of assistance. the sahel region faces numerous human rights challenges. the most conspicuous challenges include: slavery and human trafficking, weak and corrupt governance, religious extremism, and crippling poverty. in fact, four of the sahel countries rank among the six least developed countries in the world. the commission estimates that 10.3 million people are at risk of hunger in the sahel region in 2013. the conflict in mali only serves to aggravate the situation by intensifying the already prominent issues in the region as well as creating new problems specific to its own country. for example, unhcr estimates that almost 300 000 people are internally displaced in mali, with an additional 175 000 refugees fleeing to neighbouring countries. however this attention should not be to the detriment of the other chronic and persistent problems. under the cotonou agreement, both the eu and the sahel countries have mutual obligations to protect human rights and democratic principles. a greater focus on human rights is needed.
in writing. − supporting sustainable development, alongside the fight against climate change, is not only an objective of the european union's internal policies, but also a key coordinator of european policy in the world. however, this is impossible to achieve without the creation of legitimate institutional formulas for interaction, and here subsidiarity and legitimate local authorities play a major role in creating the conditions for sustainable development. at the same time, we must bear in mind the commitment that the european union has assumed in its formation and evolution as a promoter of democratic values and principles. this is impossible, however, without supporting local democracy and supporting the creation of an active, critical and engaged civil society in public policy debate or development.

in writing. i would like to welcome the adoption of this report which supports collaboration between local authorities and civil society, in line with the european union's commitment to support sustainable development. this report focuses on the need for better european cooperation between local authorities and civil society. it aims to improve the effectiveness of partnerships between all actors involved in the development of better working conditions, an agenda that supports sustainable and inclusive growth through national budgets, and by promoting the accountability of actors in the sector. the report also provides an opportunity to promote the growing involvement of marginalised groups, such as ethnic minorities, and women's organisations, in social and political dialogue and in policy preparation and implementation. i welcome the inclusion of such references in this report. indeed, they are key factors in the fight to eradicate poverty, eliminate inequalities and discrimination in employment and access to social services, and in the other 'millennium goals'.
in writing. − the relationship between european, national and local institutions must be given new impetus by the eu's initiatives to strengthen the existing network of rules and regulations. not only in the more peripheral areas, but also in the european political geography as a whole, new forms of communication between local authorities and civil society should be found in order to make the participatory process ever more inclusive and strong. in a period of severe economic and social crisis, there is a clear need to intensify and consolidate the consistency of these relations, and the european union as a whole, in conjunction with local and national authorities, can certainly play a leading role in pursuing this path.
in writing. − i welcome the european parliament's motion for a resolution on local authorities and civil society and the overall development approach it proposes. to achieve a sustainable partnership between the european union and its partners in developing countries, we need an institutionalised mechanism for dialogue between public administrations, civil society organisations, local authorities and the private sector. the european commission and the european external action service have an important role to play in the implementation of this mechanism. the added value of decentralised cooperation in the transfer of expertise and good practice from european local authorities to administrations in developing countries is immense. key areas where this partnership can be beneficial include good governance, fiscal decentralisation and sustainable development. i believe that the european union should not discriminate against civil societies in less developed countries, or in fragile countries. civil society plays a key role in all countries, regardless of their level of development.
in writing. − through this report parliament expresses great concern at the crackdown on csos cooperating with eu partners in a number of countries and calls on the commission and the eeas to develop strategies to overcome these difficulties. i want to emphasise the case of the ngos working on democratisation projects in egypt that have been closed down in 2012. these included freedom house, the international center for training of journalists and the konrad adenauer foundation. an egyptian court, after an expeditious trial, has convicted in absentia most of the employees of these ngos to five years in prison. they cannot appeal the verdict without returning to egypt and facing imprisonment. the situation of these ngo workers, three of whom are romanian and german, is very difficult. even if they have not been imprisoned, they are hostages to this conviction and cannot resume their work in the mashreq region for fear they might be extradited to egypt. these people must have a fair trial, the eeas and the commission must consider this as one of their priorities in their relations with the egyptian authorities.
in writing. − civil society organisations (csos) and local authorities are the main building blocks of smart, sustainable and inclusive development, with a view to improving living conditions both within the union and at the level of its partners. i believe that the eu's commitment to promoting a cso-friendly environment at all decision-making levels should be a model of good practice and an incentive for partner countries. moreover, local authorities have the chance to learn both from the exchanges of knowledge, which can definitely help to reduce the development gaps, on the one hand, and from the mistakes of the past of the more developed countries, in order to avoid them in the future. the participation of civil society in this process is essential. the involvement of civil society representatives in the identification and prioritisation stages gives development initiatives the necessary legitimacy. territorial development must take account in particular of the advantages and development characteristics of each region. experience at regional and local level within the eu confirms that decentralised cooperation models, multi-level governance and development partnerships have been effective tools with high added value and measurable results.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report. local government is the first level of democracy and the views of local communities, expressed through civil society or other forms, must be taken into account. local authorities must be proactive, carry out public consultation and encourage participation in decision-making. in this context, the solutions proposed in this report are welcome and useful.
in writing. − european economies and societies cannot develop without an efficient and effective education system. reducing the school drop-out rate and increasing the number of tertiary education graduates are objectives undertaken by the member states and the european union through the europe 2020 strategy. they are the premises for sustainable development and the building of an inclusive society. at the same time, overcoming many of the social divides is not possible without encouraging and facilitating dialogue between citizens from different regions. the promotion of academic mobility programmes is the instrument that contributes both to the professional development of the beneficiaries and to the intensification of the european integration process. support for educational projects and investment in education is one of the most effective ways in which the european union can contribute to combating unemployment, while at the same time being an investment and a guarantee for the future.
in writing. − in the current economic context, some of the biggest challenges are unemployment and people's ability to make a living. combating unemployment must be the main objective of the european union, and in this area education and training play an important role. in the long term, education and skills development are essential for innovation and economic growth. in the eu, unemployment among young people under 25 reached 23.5% in march 2013 but at the same time over 2 million vacancies could not be filled. this is an obvious consequence of the current situation, where the needs of the labour market are often at odds with the opportunities offered by educational institutions. in the light of the above, i believe that university-enterprise partnerships and work-based learning, as well as the development of better lifelong learning strategies, can provide new impetus for education and training reform.
in writing. − to achieve the main objectives the eu has committed to in the europe 2020 strategy, member states need to increase investment in quality education and training to train and prepare students for the ever-changing demands of the labour market. improving knowledge and skills is key, with member states needing to provide more effective education, focusing on developing creativity, cross-cultural skills (helping students to solve problems, be flexible, be able to adapt to new situations and work in teams and cross-cultural environments), practical entrepreneurial skills and science, technology, engineering and mathematics skills, including for women and from an early age, to eliminate occupational segregation and pay discrimination. public funding of education must be maintained and member states should make better use of the european structural funds and strengthen the involvement of the social partners in vocational education and training and also significantly improve the working conditions of teachers and trainers. at the same time, the commission needs to pursue a more active policy at eu level to achieve the objectives of cross-border mobility of students and workers and the transferability of qualifications.
in writing. − europe faces major challenges on the one hand, the unemployment rate among young people in the european union under the age of 25 exceeded the level of 23% in march 2013, while more than 2 million jobs remain vacant due to a lack of candidates who meet the demands of the labour market. this is partly because many job vacancies require skills that are currently held by too few young people, and partly because the demand for skilled people in fields such as science, technology, engineering and mathematics cannot be met. as such, i support the rapporteur's proposal on the need for university-enterprise partnerships and work-based learning, and the development of better lifelong learning strategies; to be able to identify the right skills for the current context - not only for students and young people entering the labour market, but also for other people who need retraining to improve their personal situation and avoid social exclusion.
we have a report that makes a number of reports on what the wide discrepancies between the education system on the one hand and the globalization system on the other hand mean in the labour market. it seems that neither the european commission nor national governments at the moment understand that they have to adapt education and new labour market requirements to what innovation, research and new employment opportunities mean in the labour market in the european union. that's why i'm asking the european commission directly to introduce a new educational paradigm at the european level through: common school textbooks, a common european timetable and the ability of national governments to take what's good in education systems, especially in the western european union. last but not least, i think it's necessary to make school uniforms compulsory to reduce social disparities. i therefore believe that the commission must intervene as a decisive decision-maker in this respect, make concrete recommendations and monitor national governments in the implementation of these measures.
in writing. − the healthcare sector is a high risk area for patient safety, with patient harm from adverse events associated with healthcare placing a heavy burden on society in this period of economic crisis. prioritizing patient safety has the potential to reduce the cost of treating patients who suffer adverse healthcare events. i believe that, in the context of an ageing european population and the worrying rise in antimicrobial resistance, patient safety, in particular the prevention and control of healthcare-associated infections, must be a priority on the political agenda of the european union as well as at national, regional and local level. member states should allocate sufficient resources to improve patient safety in order to reduce the burden of costs of treating illnesses caused by adverse events associated with healthcare.
in writing. − access to safe healthcare is the key to a quality healthcare system and is a fundamental right of european citizens. healthcare is a high-risk area, where adverse events associated with healthcare can cause serious injury, complications or suffering, or even death, to patients under treatment. it is estimated that 30-40% of adverse events associated with medical treatment in both hospitals and outpatient facilities can be prevented. it is estimated that healthcare-associated infections affect an average of 5% of hospital admissions, or 3.2 million people a year, and directly cause 37,000 deaths. patient safety contributes to improving quality of life, but the harm caused to patients by adverse events associated with healthcare is also a heavy burden on society, which is felt even more acutely in this period of economic crisis. in addition to the obvious benefits for patients, any investment in patient safety can also be a potential source of savings.
in writing. − it is currently estimated that 8-12% of patients admitted to hospital in the european union suffer adverse events associated with their treatment, whether these are infections associated with medical care, treatment-related errors, surgical errors, problems with defective or insufficiently decontaminated medical devices, diagnostic errors or lack of intervention following medical examinations. by voting today, the european parliament reaffirmed its growing concern for patient safety and reaffirmed that access to high quality healthcare is a fundamental right recognised by the european union. implementation at member state level of the council recommendations aimed at improving overall patient safety and reducing the incidence of healthcare-associated infections as a priority has yielded results, but i believe that efforts in this regard need to be further intensified as it is essential to maintain citizens' trust in the health systems of the european union. i believe that the focus should be on actions to promote research in the field of patient safety, based on an applied approach, grounded in conclusive data and focusing in particular on alternative therapies to the use of antibiotics and on the management of antibiotic resistance.
in writing. − i believe that member states should focus their efforts on improving patient safety and implement additional measures, including the establishment of action plans to combat healthcare-associated infections.
in writing. - i voted in favour of mr rossi's report because it has the merit of addressing the issue of the safety of the health system by highlighting the need for adequate training of health personnel and the allocation of adequate resources to ensure a quality service. the statistics on deaths and/or illnesses caused by inadequate safety conditions in hospital settings are worrying. i therefore believe that it is essential to take concrete action to solve the problem by improving the training of staff and, above all, by calling on the member states to allocate adequate resources. these are needs which have been fully recognised in this report, which has found a large majority in the house.
in writing. − a considerable proportion of hospitalized patients in the european union (8-12%) are victims of misdiagnosis and mismanagement. moreover, the number of elderly people who are receiving medical treatment without proper management is increasing because of a lack of specialized information or a failure to communicate it effectively. health costs to patients and health care providers can be avoided by careful health care that requires preventive treatment measures. pressure must be put on member states and local authorities to standardise the necessary requirements and to combat hai. ) thus, the council's recommendation to promote medical education among patients is welcome, to ensure their protection, perhaps even against harmful advice from medical staff. however, the best solution to protect patients and limit the costs of mci is to establish a common information system for patients and healthcare professionals who can speak the same language. thank you!
in writing. − according to recent statistics, in the european union, the financial losses caused by fraudulent marketing practices are estimated at several billion euros per year, with small and medium-sized enterprises and micro-enterprises being the main victims. although efforts have been made in recent years, both at the level of the european commission and at the level of the member states, to mitigate the serious consequences of these practices, further action is needed to counter the negative impact on economic growth. the report voted today calls on the commission to clarify the scope of the current legislative framework in this area, namely the directive on misleading and comparative advertising. the evaluations carried out on the transposition of this directive show that this legislative instrument is lacking in several respects and that an amendment is therefore necessary. as regards action at member state level, the european parliament stressed the importance of closer cooperation between national authorities and service providers. the member states were also invited to propose and promote a series of education and information initiatives to ensure that citizens and economic operators are made aware of the danger posed by these deceptive commercial practices.
in writing. − there is a clear demand from businesses, in particular smes and micro-enterprises, for better protection and effective action against fraudulent practices in a context of business-to-business relations that falls outside the scope of directive 2005/29/ec. smes, and in particular small and micro enterprises, are the main victims of deceptive marketing practices. schools, churches, hospitals, ngos and local governments, as well as other public authorities, are also targeted. thus, the investigation and prosecution of deceptive marketing practices needs to be improved, with the commission to develop guidelines for national law enforcement bodies on best practices related to investigative and prosecution priorities. member states should stimulate the capacity and expertise of investigating bodies and competent judicial authorities. it is essential that national law enforcement authorities cooperate more closely with providers whose services are used by fraudulent marketers, such as banks, telephone companies, postal services and collection agencies, in particular by enhancing the exchange of information, in order to help prevent dishonest companies from operating.
in writing. - as is well known, deceptive marketing practices can take many forms, often difficult to detect and counter. in fact, deceptive advertising has spread its tentacles everywhere, from traditional to more modern means of communication, through personal contact, through dishonest methods. the protection of the business world against deceptive advertising practices therefore requires a strict implementation of the control and prevention system and, on the other hand, a legislative system which can be as uniform as possible between european countries, so as to avoid disparities in treatment or to offer possible loopholes to those who engage in such practices that are elusive of the correct way of communicating their advertising proposal.
in writing. the european parliament resolution on misleading advertising practices is welcomed to limit, if not stop, this phenomenon, which does not bring any benefit to the european economy. it is welcome that this resolution complements directives 2006/114/ec and 2005/29/ec, especially given the different ways in which they have been transposed by the member states. to protect smes and micro-enterprises, which are at the heart of the european economy, we need a clear and unified legislative framework, but also a better exchange of information between member states, which is why i believe that the operation of national contact points can be beneficial. i welcome the commission's intention to draw up a blacklist of fraudulent practices, including a list of companies that have been convicted on several occasions for such practices. i also think that more effort is needed, especially in terms of law enforcement.

mr president, i want to express today in this plenary three feelings: appreciation, anger and disappointment. i appreciate the constant support that this house has shown to freedom of movement, and i especially appreciate the constant support for romania’s and bulgaria’s bid to join schengen. we all know that, technically, those two countries have deserved to be inside the schengen area for years now, but it has proved too good an electoral campaign theme to be passed up. i am angry at all the european politicians and parties and governments which, abusing the natural fears of their citizens due to the financial crisis, have talked about romanians and bulgarian preparing to come in huge numbers in 2014 to steal jobs and abuse the welfare systems of the host countries. what a lie. as for my disappointment, that is for the commission, which should have done more to lay to rest the nationalistic angle that now makes life difficult for many romanians and bulgarians living in other eu member states. my country, romania, may not enter schengen in 2014 due to political games, but our freedom of work will finally be equal to that of all the other eu citizens, and i will fight with all my strength to keep it that way.
mr president, i would like first to thank commissioner andor for his intervention. intra-eu mobility contributes to addressing the job mismatch and helps to even out the eu’s demographic deficit. figures show that mobile eu citizens are more likely to be of working age and more economically active than nationals. they contribute their fair share to national social security schemes. we should not let ourselves be distracted by populist speeches which create fallacious links between mobility and supposed burdens on social benefits systems. from january 2014, labour restrictions currently imposed by ten eu member states on eu citizens from romania and bulgaria will finally be lifted, and citizens from those two countries will be able to enjoy fully their right to free movement. recent studies have shown that the enlargement did not bring about any dramatic changes in immigration flows across europe. they show that mobile eu workers are net contributors to the public purse and that they tend to work in jobs where there are severe labour shortages. however, despite the crisis, the eu is faced with two million unfilled vacancies. it shows that we should keep fighting in order to ensure better matching between labour demand and supply across europe. free movement is a key factor in tackling this situation.
member of the commission. − mr president, in recent years the commission has been exploring the question of the relationship between free movement in the european union, the freedom to work in other eu countries and access to various social benefits. we have had a long dialogue, in particular with the government of the united kingdom, and in recent years we have looked into the question of increased concerns about migrating poor people, whether it is in germany, the netherlands or other countries. what i can say is that we now have a huge amount of statistics which help us to understand what exactly is happening in the member states. this supports the commission’s position, namely that there is no widespread or systematic benefit tourism in the european union. but what we also know is that we have to look behind the statistics, because it is not enough to discuss average figures, total sums or the various trends. we also need to look into individual lives. in many cases, these are people who need to find a livelihood in another country because the domestic situation is very difficult. but fundamentally, this discussion today has been about rights. we have to be very clear about what eu law allows or demands in the current context. this also needs to be clarified. for example, contrary to what mrs bizzotto said, the commission does not simply want eu citizens to move from one country to another but to have the right to move and to work in another country to be sustained and respected, together with the rights that this implies. these rights must be respected – not challenged or violated. there are also other kinds of misunderstanding, partly because of the lack of information about what the eu law says on particular issues. for example, it is a very common misunderstanding to assume that eu law would require any country to provide social benefits from day one – for example, when someone arrives in dover or any other border station. in fact, under eu law, the host countries in the eu are not obliged to grant social assistance to non-economically active eu citizens during the first three months of residence. we could look, item by item, into the specific conditions in eu legislation in order to clarify the picture, because in many cases there are examples of misinformation in the public discourse. to mr farage, i would say that it is not the individual commissioners who have to have the power but eu law which has to be powerful. eu law has to be applied in all member states. we have the responsibility to defend eu law, both in the united kingdom and in other countries. we are defending the rights of mobile eu workers in the uk, but we are also defending the rights of uk citizens when they go to other countries. for example, in spain there are 162 000 economically non-active british citizens, and when there is any kind of concern, who defends their rights? it is the commission which defends the rights of uk citizens. the most recent example of this was when we launched an infringement case in may. the commissioner requested information from spain about complaints – many of them received from uk citizens – because spanish hospitals providing public health care were refusing to recognise the european health insurance card. the commission did what the commission is supposed to do in such situations. clarifications about eu law are very important, also because eu law differentiates between eu workers and, on a temporary basis, there are different conditions for eu workers from new member states until unilateral distinctions expire. the situation of third-country nationals is also different, but sometimes the public discourse does not differentiate between them. for example, in the uk they do not take note of the fact that in recent years, net immigration was three times more than the net inward mobility from eu countries. very often, the discussion focuses on a smaller group rather than seeing the whole picture. i will not even mention eu posted workers, which is again a specific category. in order to clarify this very precisely and to ensure that it is properly implemented on the ground, the commission has launched two enforcement directives which are also before parliament and the council – one concerns the so-called eu migrants, the mobile workers, and the other the posted workers – in order to ensure that workers do not suffer abuse, either by nationals or foreigners, and that the system is not abused either by nationals or foreigners in individual member states. at the end of the day, what should also be discussed – and perhaps decided on – is what exactly the problem is. what do we have too much of in the eu – especially when some countries, as participants in this discussion have mentioned, have so-called ‘poverty migration’? is there too much poverty or too much migration? i am convinced that in the european union, there is not too much mobility. we have to expect and anticipate more mobility – hopefully more balanced mobility – but we have too much poverty. we have to do a lot more to combat poverty. we need more cooperation and more solidarity in the european union in order to tackle poverty and social exclusion. this is what i also want to emphasise to mrs weber. romania should not only fight for others to respect free movement but also do better with the absorption of eu funds, which are supposed to promote economic and social development. for example, the integration of the roma should also be supported in romania and other countries by using the european social fund and other financial instruments for better education and employment opportunities and other purposes. so, while the focus today is on rights, the subject obviously concerns not only rights but also economic development, job creation and the youth guarantee, which is a very important instrument of structural reform in order to ensure that young people also see opportunities in their own region, in their own country and not only elsewhere. if they prefer to look around elsewhere to find jobs and employment, they should have that right, and that right has to be respected. we have to expect more mobility, not least because we want to boost student mobility – mobility of learning in the european union – and that will in time lead to more professional mobility as well. but i am speaking about balanced mobility – not a flood, not an influx and not a repeat of previous experiences when, in the case of previous enlargement, there was a short period with large numbers of mobile workers coming to individual countries. why did this happen? because countries did not open up simultaneously, and then accession brought new opportunities. this will not be repeated. it has already happened with countries where there was a high potential for outward migration. that applies to poland, the baltic states and romania. but as far as romania and bulgaria are concerned, two thirds of those who left romania and bulgaria – and this was more than ten percent of the workforce in both countries – went to spain and italy, rather than the united kingdom or denmark. i believe this discussion today has been extremely helpful in clarifying the specific situations we are facing. if we are talking about poverty, we have to do more against it. if crime is the concern, of course the answer should not be the restriction of free movement or of the right to work in another country but more eu cooperation between the member states in the area of justice and law and order. this can certainly resolve some of the problems that have been observed recently.

in writing. − although used in a number of industries, such as pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, etc., drug precursors can also be used in the illicit manufacture of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. ephedrine and pseudoephedrine, substances used to manufacture medicines for various conditions such as colds and allergies, are constantly being diverted by drug traffickers from the legal trade to manufacture narcotics. the mechanisms for the control of medicinal products containing ephedrine or pseudoephedrine provided for in the regulation on the monitoring of trade in drug precursors between the community and third countries are not sufficient. it was therefore necessary to amend the provisions of the current regulation in order to improve the control of those substances and to maintain the free movement of medicinal products containing ephedrine or pseudoephedrine for legitimate purposes between the union and third countries. the first reading agreement voted by the european parliament today will help to reduce the number of attempts to divert medicines containing ephedrine or pseudoephedrine for illegal purposes. due to the improvement of the existing european legislative framework, the competent authorities of the member states will no longer have to rely on different national laws, where they exist, to intercept or confiscate such products.
in writing. − the present revision proposal aims primarily at closing a legal loophole in council regulation (ec) no 111/2005 laying down rules for the monitoring of trade in drug precursors between the eu and third countries. until now, medicinal products have always been excluded from the scope of the regulation. unfortunately, drugs containing ephedrine and pseudoephedrine, used to treat colds, flu symptoms or allergies, are diverted to synthesize methamphetamine. due to the exclusion of medicinal products from the scope of the regulation, member states face difficulties in confiscating or intercepting consignments of medicinal products containing ephedrine and pseudoephedrine which are clearly to be diverted. for this reason, the european commission decided to include medicinal products containing ephedrine and pseudoephedrine in the regulation. the competent authorities of the member states should be empowered to intercept or confiscate such products where there are reasonable grounds for suspecting that they are intended for the illicit manufacture of drugs when exported, imported or in transit.
in writing. − developments in the european union drug markets in recent years have required a revision of regulation (ec) no 273/2004 on drug precursors, in particular the provisions relating to the use of a substance called acetic anhydride (aa), which is legally used in the manufacture of perfumes, plastics and colours, but is also the main precursor to heroin. the measures proposed by the european commission and supported by both the european parliament and the council of the eu aim at better monitoring of trade in acetic anhydride (aa) and strengthening the rules on registration of this substance. the adoption of this agreement at first reading is welcome, as it will help to combat illicit drug trafficking and prevent and reduce attempts at diversion on the eu internal market, thus limiting the quantities of substances that are diverted to be used for the production of illicit drugs, specifically heroin.
in writing. − the amendments proposed to the commission regulation on drug precursors, notably acetic anhydride, make great strides toward further diminishing the presence of heroin in the member states. according to a report produced by europol earlier this year, three-quarters of drug-related deaths in europe can be linked to opioids or a combination thereof. increased cooperation and information exchange between countries and organisations have achieved significant success. the united nations office on drugs and crime convened operation tarcet in 2008 to, among other things, ‘…focus on information collection and sharing, risk profiling and analysis, and joint precursor control operations…’. under the guidance of this operation, regional authorities in central asia made numerous sizable seizures upwards of 19 tonnes of acetic anhydride, the most important precursor in heroin production. though the european market for heroin has steadily been declining over the past decade, deaths and treatment costs have remained a significant burden. by establishing more effective data parameters to optimise member state and institutional cooperation, these amendments will facilitate the further reduction in illicit drug precursor manufacturing and sales, thereby disrupting heroin markets across europe.
in writing. − improving access to justice, cooperation between judicial authorities and the effectiveness of the judiciary are key elements in the development and strengthening of the european judicial area. the introduction of information and communication technology (ict) in the administration of justice offers solutions to improve the functioning of justice, while contributing to both simplifying procedures and reducing costs. the development of e-justice is a key element of the modernisation of judicial systems. in recent years, important steps have been taken in this area, both through the launch of the e-justice portal in 2010 and through the development of tools facilitating the use of information systems in the field of justice, such as the schengen information system sis ii. the resolution voted today underlines the importance of continuing the sustained efforts made in this area by both the european commission and the member states. improving the efficiency of the judiciary and facilitating citizens' access to justice are the main objectives that the commission should consider when drawing up the future e-justice action plan for 2014-2018.
in writing. − launched in 2010, the e-justice portal needs an action plan for 2014-2018. all member states should be encouraged to participate in this action. this will facilitate open access to the use of certain eu instruments, such as the european order for payment and the european small claims procedure, as well as information systems in the field of justice and home affairs, in particular the european criminal records information system (ecris) and the schengen information system (sis) ii. e-justice systems will reduce the costs of judicial and administrative procedures, in particular by automating the exchange of information, the service of documents and the translation of certain procedural documents, in the interest of all parties in the judicial system. the provision of multilingual standard forms will thus help to reduce cross-border red tape.
in writing. − as the e-justice portal was launched in 2010, the time has come to decide on the e-justice action plan 2014-2018. the e-justice is a means of enabling increased access to legal and judicial information, as well as to judicial and administrative procedures, for both citizens and practitioners. e-justice systems tend to reduce the costs of judicial and administrative procedures, in particular by automating the exchange of information, the service of documents and the translation of certain procedural documents. this is in the interest of all stakeholders in the judiciary and, taking into account cost-effectiveness considerations, projects should remain voluntary. the eu justice programme 2014-2020 should allow for the funding of successful european and national e-justice projects that should have a real european added value for citizens. legislative work, e-justice projects and financial programming should be streamlined and it is also important to provide standard multilingual forms to reduce cross-border red tape.
on behalf of the s&d group. – mr president, today the eu is in a situation which is similar to that of the british cabinet when churchill told its members: ‘gentlemen, we have run out of money; now we must think’. that is exactly what mr brok’s report is trying to make us do: pause a little and reflect, trying to instil some order in the multitude of challenges and opportunities confronting us today. the report is correct in stating that a new world order, based on a new distribution of power, is in the making. the problem is whether we will shape it or will be shaped by it – in other words, whether it will be based on our values or on somebody else’s values. equally, the report is asking for a new and credible eu foreign policy provided, on the one hand, that we can rise above the mundane daily business making up the current substance of the eu’s external relations and, on the other hand, that it reflects truly european, not simply national strategic objectives dressed up as european interests. those truly european interests are based on relative or even similar perceptions of reality which, if they exist, facilitate the political will to act which we so often complain is lacking today. a strategic dialogue involving the council, the commission and parliament, as well as the request, formulated in the report, that the high representative / vice-president should present her foreign policy objectives for 2014 and 2015 in the next annual report, are conducive to that aim. to that effect, the report indicates specific strategies such as strengthening cooperation, particularly with regard to policies having transnational implications, and strategic policy coordination in international bodies. naturally, the cfsp and csdp get proper attention in the report. in that respect, proposals advanced by parliament in previous reports, such as common funding and more transparency in the way money is spent on operations; more effort on the part of the member states in developing and implementing the csdp; strengthening the european industrial and technological base; and more democratic scrutiny involvement of parliament, are reiterated in the report. another contribution, which is also a step forward, is the report’s recommendation that european defence should be firmly based on the revised european security strategy and a white book which should serve as a common template for concurrent national security and defence reviews – this being, after all, the case in all member states. in conclusion – apart from congratulating the rapporteur – i would point to the very good communication and cooperation of the author with the shadow rapporteurs and his willingness to accommodate as many views as possible and find common ground between them.
mr president, beside all the good things that i could mention, let me say that the european union foreign and security policy is held hostage by the dilemma of choosing between values and geostrategy. this is a false dilemma, since values are a dimension of power and part of the geopolitical endeavour. eu interests are best protected in areas and with partners sharing the same values. however, the promotion of eu values must not be done at the expense of geopolitical interests, and vice versa. both are about the security of european citizens. the real problem lies in our failure to understand that our values cannot prevail until we prevail in the geostrategic race. this does not mean that we should abandon our values for the sake of a geostrategic rationale. it means that first we have to create a security framework for those values to grow. the prevalence we currently give to our values does not reflect our attachment to them but our ineffectiveness in defining our geostrategic identity and therefore our long-term interest and geopolitical goals. we are fighting an elusive crusade that gives us a false impression that we are imposing our model around the world while disguising the real reactive character of our external action. you must overcome this messiah complex and stop behaving as a global secular priesthood. likewise, we must admit that the more-for-more approach does not function when the countries concerned have geopolitical or geo-economic alternatives. a foreign policy without strategic goals is a vehicle going nowhere. like alice in wonderland, we fool ourselves that if we do not know the destination, all roads will lead us there. if we do not change that, we will condemn ourselves to irrelevance. a soft power, yes; but a soft power with vision and teeth. this is what we need to be.
